idiom_name: reply channel + correlation identifier + reply deadline and cancellation hook
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every request a reply address (a private or anonymous queue, a callback continuation, an in-process port) or a correlation token that the replier echoes, plus an explicit deadline and a cancellation rule. Structure the requestor as a pending table keyed by correlation id whose entries hold the waiter (a future, callback or blocked thread), and make the reply handler dispatch each arriving reply to exactly one entry, removing it atomically. On timeout or cancellation remove the entry and record the exchange as failed; a reply that arrives later is dropped or dead-lettered, never delivered to a reused entry. Define whether the operation is idempotent, because the caller may time out after the replier already performed the work.
code_sketch:
pending = {}                          # correlation id -> waiter/future
on reply(reply_channel):               # demultiplex by token
    w = pending.pop(reply.corr_id, None)
    if w: w.complete(reply.payload)    # unknown/late replies are dropped
send(request, reply_to=my_address, corr_id=new_id(), deadline=now()+5s)
try:    return await_or_block(pending[corr_id], deadline)
finally: pending.pop(corr_id, None)  # abandon on timeout/cancel
pitfalls: Correlating by arrival order or payload content instead of a token: retries and concurrency silently mis-associate replies.
A pending entry that is not removed on every exit path leaks and can be woken by a late reply.
No deadline: one lost reply parks the caller forever and the pending table grows without bound.
Non-idempotent repliers: the caller's timeout does not stop the work, so a retry can double-apply effects.

Wrong move: treat a deadline expiry as rollback -> the replier may already have completed work before the caller observes the timeout, so a retry can duplicate effects -> instead propagate cancellation where supported and make the operation idempotent or deduplicate by request id.
